name: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections

clinicalPearls: Human fungal disease has risen sharply with the AIDS pandemic, broad antibacterial use, cytotoxic chemotherapy, biologic/precision-medicine immunosuppressants, and solid-organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (Harrison 22e p.1687).

Mycoses are categorized clinically as mucocutaneous versus deep-organ disease, and epidemiologically as endemic versus opportunistic; mucocutaneous disease causes morbidity but is rarely fatal, whereas deep-organ disease is often severe with high mortality (Harrison 22e p.1687).

Endemic fungi are environmentally acquired and not part of normal flora, typically causing self-limited disease in immunocompetent hosts but severe illness when immunity is impaired; opportunistic fungi such as Candida and Aspergillus are commensal or ubiquitous and invade when host defenses fail (Harrison 22e p.1687).

Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic demonstration of the fungus invading tissue together with culture from the specimen; a positive culture from blood or tissue can instead reflect colonization or laboratory contamination depending on organism and site (Harrison 22e p.1690).

PAS and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) are the principal fungal stains; Candida (unlike most fungi) is visible on Gram-stained tissue, and a positive India ink stain of CSF is diagnostic for cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1690).

The most reliable antigen/serologic tests are Coccidioides antibody, Histoplasma antigen, and cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen; galactomannan (best in BAL fluid) aids aspergillosis diagnosis but has frequent false negatives during antifungal prophylaxis and false positives with other fungi (Harrison 22e p.1691).

The serum beta-D-glucan assay has a high negative predictive value for invasive candidiasis but lacks specificity, and T2 magnetic resonance is FDA-approved for detecting Candida in blood (Harrison 22e p.1691).

Inherited CARD9 deficiency is the only known primary immunodeficiency that produces fungus-specific susceptibility without predisposition to other infections, autoimmunity, allergy, or cancer, causing chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, CNS Candida/Aspergillus/phaeohyphomycete infection, and deep dermatophytosis (Harrison 22e p.1688).

Antifungal host defense is compartmentalized: IL-17-producing lymphoid cells protect mucosal surfaces against Candida invasion, neutrophils control invasive Aspergillus and Candida, and the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis with activated macrophages controls intramacrophagic fungi such as Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, and endemic dimorphic fungi (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689).

AIDS predisposes to mucosal but not invasive candidiasis (reflecting IL-17 dependence), whereas vaginal candidiasis arises with antibiotic use rather than AIDS or IL-17-targeted biologics, highlighting the protective role of the vaginal microbiota (Harrison 22e p.1689).

Chronic granulomatous disease, caused by NADPH-oxidase subunit mutations impairing neutrophil superoxide generation, carries roughly a 40% lifetime risk of invasive aspergillosis; Aspergillus nidulans is seen almost exclusively in this condition (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689).

Early initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy is a key determinant of outcome in candidemia, aspergillosis, and mucormycosis, alongside source control (catheter removal in candidemia, abscess drainage, surgical debridement in mucormycosis) and immune reconstitution (Harrison 22e p.1691).
harrison.pathophysiology: Fungi are eukaryotes classified morphologically as yeasts (round/budding single cells), molds (filamentous hyphae at both room temperature and in tissue, e.g., Aspergillus, Mucorales, dermatophytes), and dimorphic fungi (yeast or spherical structures in tissue but filamentous forms in the environment). Candida produces both yeast and pseudohyphal forms in tissue except C. glabrata and C. auris, which form only yeasts; Cryptococcus exists only as yeast. Deep-organ infection by molds and endemic dimorphic fungi follows inhalation, whereas commensal Candida invades from mucocutaneous colonization in the gut or skin. Antifungal immunity centers on the C-type lectin receptor/SYK/CARD9 signaling pathway, which recognizes fungal polysaccharides and drives proinflammatory mediator release, leukocyte recruitment, inflammasome activation, and Th17 differentiation. Protection is site- and pathogen-specific: at mucosa, IL-17A/IL-17F and IL-22 from Th17, Tc17, gamma-delta T, and innate lymphoid cells stimulate epithelial antimicrobial peptide production and barrier repair (STAT3-dependent); against invasive molds and Candida, recruited neutrophils assemble the six-subunit NADPH oxidase to generate superoxide for fungal killing; against intramacrophagic fungi, IL-12-producing macrophages activate STAT4 in T cells to release IFN-gamma, which signals through STAT1 (with TNF-alpha and GM-CSF) to enable intracellular killing. Defects at any node, whether inherited (e.g., IL17F/IL17RA/IL17RC/TRAF3IP2, STAT3, STAT1, CARD9, NADPH oxidase subunits, IL12RB1, IFNGR1/2, IRF8, GATA2) or pharmacologic/acquired (IL-17/IL-23 biologics, BTK inhibitors, glucocorticoids, anti-TNF agents, JAK inhibitors, anti-IFN-gamma or anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies), produce predictable, compartment-specific fungal susceptibility (Harrison 22e pp.1687-1689).
additionalDifferentials: Distinguishing true invasive fungal infection from colonization or laboratory contamination when fungi are recovered from culture (Harrison 22e p.1690)
Chronic cavitary pulmonary mycosis versus cavitary tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1690)
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis versus invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in differing host settings (Harrison 22e p.1688)
infectionMimics: Mycobacterial infection (notably tuberculosis), which shares granulomatous histology and intramacrophagic survival with endemic dimorphic fungi (Harrison 22e p.1689)
Salmonellosis and other intramacrophagic pathogens that exploit the same IL-12/IFN-gamma defects as intramacrophagic fungi (Harrison 22e p.1689)
nonInfectiousMimics: Neoplasia and other causes of granulomatous or necrotizing tissue reaction (H&E-defined granuloma, angioinvasion, necrosis are nonspecific without organism identification) (Harrison 22e p.1690)
Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous conditions in patients predisposed to cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1688)
additionalInvestigations: Histopathology with PAS and GMS stains, plus H&E to assess granuloma, angioinvasion, and necrosis (Harrison 22e p.1690)
Calcofluor white staining with fluorescence microscopy for fungi in fluid specimens (Harrison 22e p.1690)
Lysis-centrifugation blood culture to increase sensitivity for Candida and less common fungi such as Histoplasma (Harrison 22e p.1690)
MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for detection and speciation of cultured fungi (Harrison 22e pp.1690-1691)
Antigen and serologic assays: cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen, Histoplasma antigen, Coccidioides antibody, galactomannan (BAL preferred), and serum beta-D-glucan (Harrison 22e p.1691)
T2 magnetic resonance assay for Candida in whole blood (Harrison 22e p.1691)
India ink stain of CSF, diagnostic for cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1690)
redFlags: Profound or prolonged neutropenia, allogeneic HSCT, or high-dose glucocorticoids portend invasive mold disease (aspergillosis, mucormycosis) and invasive candidiasis (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689)
Diabetic ketoacidosis as a setting for rhinocerebral/sinopulmonary mucormycosis (Harrison 22e p.1688)
Advanced AIDS with low CD4 counts predisposing to intramacrophagic and mucosal mycoses (Harrison 22e p.1689)
Delay in appropriate antifungal therapy in candidemia, aspergillosis, or mucormycosis, which worsens outcome (Harrison 22e p.1691)
Failure to achieve source control (retained central venous catheter in candidemia, undrained abscess, undebrided necrotic sinus tissue in mucormycosis) (Harrison 22e p.1691)
Emerging drug-resistant species: azole/echinocandin-resistant Candida glabrata, Candida auris, and azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (Harrison 22e p.1687)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome hinges on host immune status, the fungus and site involved, timeliness of appropriate therapy, source control, and immune reconstitution. Mucocutaneous mycoses cause morbidity but are rarely fatal, whereas deep-organ infections are frequently severe with high mortality. Before amphotericin B, cryptococcal meningitis and other disseminated mycoses were nearly always fatal. A favorable prognosis in opportunistic mycoses depends substantially on restoring host immunity, for example neutrophil recovery, tapering of immunosuppression, or starting combination antiretroviral therapy in AIDS (Harrison 22e pp.1687, 1691).
pitfalls: Treating a positive fungal culture as proof of infection when it may represent colonization or contamination, depending on organism and anatomic site (Harrison 22e p.1690)
Relying on galactomannan for aspergillosis without accounting for frequent false negatives under antifungal prophylaxis and false positives from other fungi (Harrison 22e p.1691)
Interpreting a beta-D-glucan result without recognizing its lack of specificity despite a high negative predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1691)
Attempting to identify fungi reliably on H&E alone, which defines tissue reaction but is insufficient for speciation (Harrison 22e p.1690)

Overlooking that fluconazole and echinocandins lack activity against molds (and echinocandins against Cryptococcus and endemic dimorphic fungi), and that voriconazole/echinocandins do not cover Mucorales (Harrison 22e pp.1691-1692)
Failing to monitor drug levels where pharmacokinetics are variable (e.g., itraconazole capsules, voriconazole with CYP2C19 polymorphism) (Harrison 22e pp.1691-1692)

Not recognizing that emerging immunomodulatory biologics (IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors, BTK inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, anti-TNF, SYK inhibitors) create predictable, compartment-specific fungal risk (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689)
harrison.severityClassification: Classified by anatomic depth (mucocutaneous infections, which are rarely fatal, versus deep-organ infections, which are severe and often highly fatal) and by epidemiologic category (endemic versus opportunistic). Severity within these groups is further modulated by host immune competence, the implicated fungus, and the involved tissue (Harrison 22e p.1687).
management: Select antifungal therapy by fungal class and site: echinocandins or azoles for invasive candidiasis, an azole such as voriconazole or isavuconazole or a polyene for invasive aspergillosis, and amphotericin B with flucytosine for cryptococcal disease
Treat mucormycosis with liposomal amphotericin B alongside urgent surgical debridement, as antifungal drugs alone are insufficient
Achieve source control by removing infected intravascular catheters, draining collections and debriding angioinvasive or necrotic tissue
Restore host defences where possible by reducing immunosuppression, reversing neutropenia and pursuing immune reconstitution
Monitor azole therapy with therapeutic drug concentrations and for hepatotoxicity and drug interactions, and track response with serial antigen or beta-D-glucan assays
Distinguish colonisation from invasive disease before committing to prolonged therapy, and tailor treatment duration to organism, site and immune recovery
Manage endemic mycoses by severity, using an azole for mild-to-moderate disease and polyene induction for severe or disseminated infection
Involve infectious diseases specialists and, for deep-organ disease, the relevant surgical teams
